---
title: "Knapsack: Take or Skip the Current Item"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning with small numerical examples."
---

## When to recognise the pattern

When each item can be used at most once and you choose a subset under a capacity.

## The key question

**How can one recurrence describe all possible subsets without listing every subset?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
D(i,c)=\max\{D(i-1,c),\,v_i+D(i-1,c-w_i)\}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** D(i,c) is the maximum value obtainable from the first i items with capacity c; item i has value v_i and weight w_i; max selects the better of skipping and taking it. The second option exists only when w_i≤c.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Suppose item 1 has weight 2,value 3 and item 2 has weight 3,value 4; capacity c=3. Skip item 2: D(1,3)=3. Take item 2: value 4 plus D(1,0)=0, so max(3,4)=4.

## Why this is mathematically correct

Any feasible subset either contains the last item or does not. These cases cover every subset, and within each case an optimal remainder must itself be optimal; otherwise replacing it would improve the solution.

## Limits and counterexamples

This is 0/1 knapsack. If repetition is allowed, the take-case remainder may stay at i instead of i−1. Be explicit about zero-weight items and whether value can be negative.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Last item is either absent or present. Write both feasible branches and take max, then establish base case D(0,c)=0.**

Now reproduce the equation, example and proof aloud, without looking.

**Interview problems:** Partition Equal Subset Sum; 0/1 Knapsack.
